value.overview: The Plain-capped Starthroat is a large hummingbird of dry forests, woodland edges, thorn scrub, and other open habitats in Mexico and Central America. Its plumage is mostly green, gray, and brown, and the male has a small reddish or rose-colored throat patch that can be difficult to see. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon species associated mainly with the drier northwestern Pacific region, although records also occur elsewhere.
value.classification: The Plain-capped Starthroat belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Heliomaster. It is one of the mountain-gem hummingbirds and is sometimes placed with the starthroats as a distinct group.
value.identification: This is a relatively large hummingbird, about 10–15 cm long, with a long, straight bill, a dull green back, and pale grayish or buff underparts. A broad white whisker stripe and a white patch near the rump or wing base are useful field marks. Adult males have a reddish throat center bordered by darker feathers, but the color may be inconspicuous in poor light. Females and immature birds are duller and lack a strongly visible gorget.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from western and southern Mexico through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and into northwestern Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is most reliably associated with dry forest, scrub, woodland edges, open hillsides, gardens, and flowering trees, especially in Guanacaste and adjacent northwestern areas. It is generally found at low elevations, although occasional records have come from higher sites and from other provinces, indicating some dispersal beyond its usual Costa Rican range.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Plain-capped Starthroat is best treated as a resident or irregular seasonal species rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may follow flowering and rainfall, and the species appears to be more regularly encountered in the dry northwest. Records elsewhere in Costa Rica may represent dispersal, seasonal movements, or occasional wandering; the extent of migration remains poorly documented.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited. In Costa Rica, nesting has been reported or inferred mainly from October through January, during part of the seasonal transition into the dry season. The nest is a small, shallow cup made from plant fibers and soft down, often decorated with lichens and placed on a slender branch. As with other hummingbirds, the female is expected to handle incubation and chick rearing, while the male does not provide parental care.
value.dietFeeding: The Plain-capped Starthroat feeds primarily on nectar from flowering trees, shrubs, vines, and other plants, especially in open or seasonally dry habitats. Its long bill allows it to use tubular flowers. It also captures small insects and other arthropods, either by short aerial sallies or while moving among vegetation. It may defend productive flowers or feeding areas from other hummingbirds and is often seen hovering briefly before perching.
value.behavior: This hummingbird usually forages in open woodland, forest edges, scrub, and clearings rather than in dense forest interiors. It often perches conspicuously on exposed twigs and makes rapid, direct flights between feeding sites. Displays and chases can occur around flowers or territories. The species is generally quiet or gives sharp chips and high, thin calls, and its subdued plumage can make it easy to overlook despite its fairly large size.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is believed to be declining, but the decline is not currently considered severe enough to place the species in a threatened IUCN category.
